title: The Nature of the Psalm and the Sinners
english: The awareness of one's own evils and the knowledge of God's goodness leads to the prayer, 'Have mercy on me and see the humiliation that has come upon me from my enemies' (Ps 9:15b). For they humiliated me by dragging me down; but You alone are able to lift me up from the gates of death through a goodness that is essentially present.

Regarding the daughters of Zion, those participating in this must hear in harmony with being called sons of light, peace, and wisdom. The gates of the daughter of Zion, being opposite the gates of death, are praiseworthy deeds and contemplations of God's virtue and wisdom to be fulfilled.

Concerning the incorruptible virtue, it is said: 'The grace [is] with those who love our Lord Jesus Christ in incorruption' (Ps 9:16), while the opposite, evil, will be called corruption and destruction. It is shown that corruption is called evil from the saying, 'If anyone destroys the temple of God' (1 Cor 3:17), and from what is said to the wicked in the prophet, 'Because of incorruption you have been corrupted by destruction.' This is consistent with, 'Who will help you against your corruption, O Israel?' (Hos 4:9). The corruption so spoken of, in the doing of what is, is promised to be accomplished by those who possess it. The word says that the mortals have fallen into that in which they practiced corruption (Ps 7:15). For no one else is seized by another's impiety and sin; for each one dies by his own sin.

And since the wicked, having first harmed themselves and others through deceit, attempt to bring the same harm by trial, they secretly prepare snares in their treacherous wisdoms and words to catch the unsuspecting. By that very snare they are punished. For they render justice and through those whom they deceived. And to suffer thus becomes a judgment of the provident God; for how is it not His judgment that, in His works, He seizes the sinner who has used the pretext of acting wickedly to be condemned from without? This is consistent with what was said a little earlier: 'He who digs a pit will fall into it' (Ps 7:15). Having spoken about the psalm of lament, the song of the lament must now be spoken. Having begun the present psalm from 'I will confess to You, Lord,' the proclamation extended as 'The sinner was caught'; after which the words of the song [begin]...

Since 'Let the sinners be turned away' follows the interlude, the name of the hymn is entwined with the interlude. For if the whole psalm is called a hymn, the preface of the hymn was always arranged in a way and with a power before it, as is demonstrated for many psalms. But since it is not so here, and since the beginning is taken after the interlude, it is fitting that 'Hymn of the interlude' be placed in between. It will be shown how the hymn possesses the thought of the following, with their words being set forth: 'Let the sinners be turned away' etc. Ps 9:18–19: 'Let the sinners be turned away, those imposing judgment against the righteous, into the abyss.'

Interpreting who the sinners are, he brought forward that the things being forgotten are mortal things of God. But sinners and mortals must be understood not as men only, but also as fleshless powers. For if the sinner does not signify essence, but rather what kind of voice the sinner is—a nickname not from the sin itself—then everyone participating in sin would not be called thus. Appropriately to these things, the mortals will also be called. Just as one who is not locally in heaven, but walking upon the earth, is able to possess citizenship and thought there, so also one not dwelling locally in the abyss is able to bear signs of death and of sinning himself, as if he dwells in the abyss, even though he is among those in the life after the body.

And he is called poor, the one impoverishing through sin, and the moderate and the foolish, and the one needing to receive from God; and such a one is born wretched. According to all these ways, the one called poor is remembered by God. For through something advantageous, some forgetfulness of him might occur, but it does not remain entirely so, and for this reason he will not be forgotten unto the end. As for who will be judged poor or needy, we will say as the opportunity calls us to speak about these things. Ps 9:20: 'You, Lord, make those who stagger and those who faint fall from the lofty height, opposing the proud; let them not then be strong, but let them be judged before you; for a surpassing benefit will spring forth for them.'

Let it be interpreted that 'Let man not be strong' as it was said concerning the devil, and it is said in the parable of the tares as being an enemy of man, but also in the prophecy: 'Not man is the one provoking the earth.' And since man was not being strong before the descent of the Savior, saying...
translator_notes: True OET; Pass A ≠ Pass B. Melito skipped; never Cyril Matthew densify.

title: The Provocation of God and the Nature of Sin
english: I will take the inhabited world in my hand as a disease and as abandoned dust to wipe away; no one shall escape me or answer me.

The human race does not bring the words of its pride as an embassy to the Savior, saying, 'Arise, O Lord, descend to us, so that the human who is proud against us may not be strengthened for long.' For the devil says that 'man' is not a mortal rational animal, but that they have fallen away from divinity just as those to whom God said, 'I am; you are gods and all are sons of the Most High, but you, as men, die' (Ps 82:6).

The prophet asks like a man and inquires of God, saying, 'Why, Lord, have you stood far off?' (Ps 22:13). If the Word responds to him, what is the good of God for the repentance of sinners? For God has stood far from the sinners, His presence discerning the sin itself and driving the sinners far away according to what has been said: 'Your sins divide [you] between me and you' (Ps 83:15). Otherwise, God is always present to all and happens to fill all things everywhere. Therefore it has been said in the prophecies: 'I am a God approaching,' says the Lord, 'and not a God from afar.'

But for the righteous who are afflicted in the present life and oppressed by the ungodly, he says, 'As if standing far off, you abandon them, O Lord, and look down from above' (Ps 22:14). Consequently, the pride of the ungodly increases, while He burns your poor and wretched one, the God-fearing man, who zealously desires and inwardly burns the soul with zeal.

And especially those who are deprived of divine wealth and wisdom and are not precise concerning the doctrines of piety; for they do not stumble upon judgments praising the sinner for that which he desires, it being manifest that the sinner reaches out not for the heretical but for the pleasant and the passionate. Along with these, they consider wealth and human, fleeting glory to be a blessing from the same error, asserting that the wrongdoers are blessed by God; but it is necessary to examine how the blessing of God is given to the righteous.
Even if it has seemed that God stands far off and looks down from above on the afflicted because of being troubled by the pride of the ungodly...

But he does not very much rage against the proud one having stumbled and, if it is said according to the scripture, having set fire to the poor man because of the bad use of the things that were to him by God's providence. For this is shown from the following words: for it is said, 'The sinner provoked the Lord.' And the one provoking is the impious one, praising himself according to his own desires. And he provoked the Lord to such an extent as for the anger to become stretched out, that he himself has stored up for himself according to what was said, 'According to your hardness and unrepentant heart, you store up for yourself wrath in a day of wrath' (Ps 7:16).

However, even if much wrath has been stored up by him, nevertheless there will not be a search according to the abundance and greatness of it on the day of judgment because of the goodness of the judging God. For if a search according to the abundance of the wrath were to happen, the wicked would immediately be lost. Having seen this very thing, they say, regarding the goodness being shown: 'If iniquity is observed, Lord, Lord, who will endure?' (Ps 53:2). The pretext for the sinner provoking the Lord is not having him before the eyes and in the presence, since he has turned away from God. For every one sinning does this; therefore God says concerning every such one, 'They turned their backs on me, and not faces' (Ps 53:2).

Cain, having become the father of this impiety, 'Went out from the presence of the Lord God, having turned away from him' (Gen 4:16) clearly. If these things are said concerning sinful men, much more concerning the devil, having provoked God and not having him before him. For especially the following words are said concerning him: 'His ways are defiled at all times' (Ps 106:18). For whose ways are defiled at all times, except of the impious, habitually performing many, many things? And he walks impiously, not only in single acts seizing men, but also defining unprovidence.

Indeed, he has persuaded many to dogmatize the unprotected world, having first himself fallen from the right opinion concerning God's administration and judgment. This is shown from what is said to God concerning him, 'Your judgments are overthrown from his face; he shall lord it over all his enemies' (Ps 72:4), not as if he were going to do this always, but because this very thing is set forth; for it is a lie...
translator_notes: True OET; Pass A ≠ Pass B. Melito skipped; never Cyril Matthew densify.

title: The Hidden Danger of the Rich and the Protection of the Poor
english: He will be Lord over all his enemies. For especially his enemies are those perfect in holiness in whom no one rules. But he rules over only those practicing sin; for it is said, 'Everyone practicing sin is a slave to sin.' And the slave of sin is ruled over by the devil, who has worked sin in him. And according to the insatiable nature of his wickedness, what follows is brought forth: 'For if indeed,' he says, 'I shall never be shaken from generation to generation by evil' (Ps 9:28). The word reveals his arrogance together with impudence. By this voice, one having understood will interpret regarding only those humans who have become his enemies, to say that he will rule over all his enemies. For if indeed from generation to generation one has never been shaken in heart by evil, it is evident that the saying refers only to humans having the 'being' in succession. But even this is not entirely true; for he did not rule over the holy patriarchs and prophets and apostles; rather, they themselves stretched out this authority under the feet of Jesus.

He, having fallen away from his holiness, truth, and blessing, leading himself far away, has a mouth full of curses, through which he says, testing, making a punishment and a curse upon those being deceived. And his word has much wickedness along with the harm; therefore, along with the curse and bitterness and deceit, his word is full, being called his mouth. And since he brings forth none of these things to harm and destroy under his tongue, but the word itself is harmful, pain and toil exist; for nothing is gentle or kind, but if he brings in toil and pain, he brings it forth.

Setting before himself harm and destruction through all things, he chooses men appearing to be rich in word (having pseudonymous knowledge), and sitting with them, he tries to sit hidden so as to remain unknown, to kill the innocent by wounding him with his burning arrows (Ps 9:29-32); for these are things scattering death, striking the one being cast from the life with virtue by the arrows. It is possible to pierce and thus: 'He sits in a seat with...'

Of the rich; with the stichoi we bring forward 'To kill the innocent in secret.' For the 'in secret' part causes doubt, being divided in two ways, as we have previously noted by stichoi: 'He sits in the seat with the rich in secret' (Ps 2:6), [followed by] 'to kill the innocent.' However, even if he sits in a seat with the aforementioned rich, intending to look and to kill the innocent, it is necessary to oversee that no one of the God-wise may be able to wound one clothed in the panoply of God; for he, obeying the command to turn his eyes toward the poor man, has him captured, the same one acting toward the poor man being scorched by the impiety of the ungodly's pride.

He sits in secret, a fierce lion in his den, to snatch the poor man through deceptive words (and indeed also through deeds), and he will drag him after snatching him into his trap in order to devour him. For he is a fierce beast, rather even a lion. Often indeed, sitting in a seat and seemingly speaking about stewardship, he conceals the matter concerning love of money. As one speaking about temperance, he proposes a manner of intemperance, just as the serpent deceived Eve in the paradise through the transgression of the commandment, setting up equality, and likewise Judas through love of money. The 'looking down' written there shows that, having turned the eye downward, he fell; for how could he not direct his gaze downward, he who rejects Providence, by saying 'God has forgotten' and the following things? (Ps 9:35–37a)

Being able immediately to humble the proud one who tyrannizes those being shaken by his audacity, for what is the use, being able to help them, if you allow them a certain time to be afflicted, during which you understood not only the pain upon him and through him? And this has happened, so that those who have benefited through the timely affliction may willingly deliver themselves into your hands, having a remaining desire to be disciplined and to be ruled by you. To you, then, the poor man is not abandoned; you will manage the things concerning his salvation, so that you may make him rich by providing good things from heaven. So also he helps the orphan, presiding over and rearing him into the rank of a son. An orphan in these things...
translator_notes: True OET; Pass A ≠ Pass B. Melito skipped; never Cyril Matthew densify.
